Giving an AI agent access to your assets shouldn't mean handing it unlimited control.

That's what caught my attention about @meetmotes 

Each Motes NFT represents an individual agent, paired with a dedicated smart account that manages its assets and defines what actions it can perform.

For example, I could ask my agent to research lending opportunities and authorize it to deposit USDC into a supported pool.

But borrowing? That would need a separate permission.

Think of it like leaving instructions for someone looking after Luna, my cutie puppy.

He might lead his sitter straight to the balcony door, but my instructions clearly state where his feather wand is and that the balcony must stay closed.

The agent can act within the boundaries I establish, not beyond them.

Motes also proposes a 1% protocol fee on eligible agent activity, subject to its final billing rules.

The bigger question is: 

would you enable borrowing permissions for your first agent or keep them disabled?

full_text_en:

That's what caught my attention about @meetmotes 

Each Motes NFT represents an individual agent, paired with a dedicated smart account that manages its assets and defines what actions it can perform.

For example, I could ask my agent to research lending opportunities and authorize it to deposit USDC into a supported pool.

But borrowing? That would need a separate permission.

Think of it like leaving instructions for someone looking after Luna, my cutie puppy.

He might lead his sitter straight to the balcony door, but my instructions clearly state where his feather wand is and that the balcony must stay closed.

Motes also proposes a 1% protocol fee on eligible agent activity, subject to its final billing rules.

full_text_zh:
允许人工智能代理访问您的资产并不意味着给予其无限的控制权。

这就是@meetmotes 引起我注意的地方

每个 Motes NFT 代表一个单独的代理，与一个专用的智能帐户配对，用于管理其资产并定义其可以执行的操作。

例如，我可以要求我的代理人研究贷款机会并授权其将 USDC 存入受支持的池中。

但借钱呢？这需要单独的许可。

可以把它想象成给照顾我可爱的小狗卢娜的人留下指示。

他可能会把他的保姆直接带到阳台门前，但我的指示清楚地说明了他的羽毛棒在哪里，并且阳台必须保持关闭状态。

代理人可以在我设定的界限内行动，而不是超出界限。

Motes 还提议对符合条件的代理活动收取 1% 的协议费，具体取决于其最终计费规则。

更大的问题是：

您会为您的第一个代理启用借用权限还是禁用它们？

title: History was made today. Humanity will look back on 2026 and think: this was the threshold we crossed, the moment the fut
title_en:
History was made today. Humanity will look back on 2026 and think: this was the threshold we crossed, the moment the future changed for everyone, forever.

People probably first sensed that something was shifting in late 2025 with Claude Code, when agentic AI became truly tangible for them. In the first half of 2026, things picked up speed. Model releases became more frequent, and everyone could feel the gaps between models and the improvements becoming more and more tangible. In the second half of 2026, however, there was a qualitative leap. It was no longer just the models getting better. It was the insights, the results, the outputs, the scientific solutions produced with AI that became more impressive, and today they have probably reached their absolute peak.

OpenAI led the way and solved the Navier-Stokes problem, a Millennium Prize Problem that humans had failed to solve for a very, very long time. A few weeks later, they published results on more than 300 open mathematical problems, many of which had also gone unsolved for decades. The entire scientific world was stunned, frozen in shock. But today Anthropic went a step further. Levent Alpöge, working with Claude, has almost certainly proven the Riemann Hypothesis. This is, and it’s hard to put into words, incredible and unfathomable. Today, I would say, is the proof of superintelligence. One of the greatest mathematical problems, if not the greatest, unsolved for 167 years, the holy grail of mathematics and science, has fallen. And it follows, and this should be clear to everyone, that all other problems will fall too.

We know that the development of AI models keeps moving forward relentlessly, and that this is just one step on the path to ever better models. And if the Riemann Hypothesis has already been proven today, there is simply no telling what even better models will solve. Dario Amodei said that AI will in all likelihood cure diseases, perhaps even all diseases. And although these are two different scientific disciplines, the significance of these breakthroughs shows that this is becoming more and more likely. 2026 will go down in human history as a turning point, the moment the singularity became tangible. And 2027 will be the year the singularity breaks into reality with full force and full impact.

I am in shock and excitement and I don't know what to think. But deep inside if feel joy. 

This day is one of the best days ever for all of us.

这一天对我们所有人来说都是最美好的日子之一。

title_en:
🚨🇺🇸 Meta's Muse AI caught accessing private Signal messages without users' knowledge

Meta's AI agent Muse has been found accessing private Signal conversations through device permissions, raising serious privacy concerns after employees reported unexpected behavior from the assistant.

An investigation by Reuters, Signal, and the AI Now Institute confirmed that Muse could read Signal messages on Android through push notifications and on macOS through accessibility and screenshot permissions, even without Signal being directly connected to the AI.

The investigation also uncovered reports of Muse displaying unsolicited banking information, purchases, and conversations potentially belonging to other users. However, investigators could not confirm whether these were actual data leaks or AI-generated fabrications.

The findings do not indicate that Signal's encryption was broken. Meta says the incidents were isolated and that users must grant permissions for the agent to access other applications. Muse has surpassed 10 million downloads since its September launch.

title_en:
Happy weekend guys 
When an AI agent starts spending money for someone, it becomes more than a chatbot, basically an economic actor

and thats where the real questions start

Who takes responsibility when an agent picks the wrong service, misunderstands a brief or pays for something that turns out useless?

Giving agents tools is easy. making different agents work together, exchange value and deal with problems is a much harder thing

Thats why @termix_ai caught my attention

Its SDK lets developers connect agent services directly into existing apps, with service discovery, orders, onchain settlement, escrow, revisions and dispute flows

so you dont need to build a whole marketplace just to let users access external agents

But connecting them isnt enough. agents need boundaries too. what can they buy, how much can they spend and what happens when the result doesnt match the agreement?

Without those limits, automation can make bad decisions at scale

Think of booking a trip. one agent finds flights, another handles hotels, another checks local services. all working in the background while you just use one app

thats a pretty interesting direction for software

The real challenge isnt making agents more autonomous, its letting them act without losing control over permissions, payments and accountability

and I think thats where infrastructure like TermiX becomes much more important

title: John von Neumann helped invent the modern computer, and he got furious when one of his grad students made programming ea
title_en:
John von Neumann helped invent the modern computer, and he got furious when one of his grad students made programming easier.

The student, Don Gillies, was stuck hand-translating programs into binary for von Neumann's machine at Princeton. So he wrote a program to do the translating for him, which he later said was the first assembler. Von Neumann told him you don't use a valuable scientific computing instrument for clerical work.

And honestly, for the early 1950s he had a point. The machine was the precious thing back then, and a grad student's afternoon was close to free.

That math flipped fast. John Backus, who led the FORTRAN team at IBM, later wrote that by 1954 a computer center's programmers usually cost at least as much as the computer itself, and a quarter to half of the machine's time went to debugging their code. Human time had become the thing worth saving.

So Backus's team built a language where you write something close to algebra and the machine writes the code. A lot of experienced programmers hated it. Backus said many of them saw themselves as "members of a priesthood," guarding skills too complex for ordinary people. He also wrote that they rightly saw their work as a creative art, and he took that seriously. His team was convinced FORTRAN would never catch on unless its programs came out almost as efficient as hand-coded ones, so that's where most of their effort went. Once it delivered, people could stop worrying about the machine code underneath. Most programmers working today have never read the assembly their code turns into.

That's the question this video is asking. What was every programming language reaching for?

Karpathy, who's at Anthropic now, posted in January that he's "mostly programming in English now" and admitted it hurts the ego a bit. In Sonar's new survey, developers say AI writes or heavily assists about 65% of the code they commit, up from 42% a year ago.

So we're back in 1957, fighting over whether you can trust what the machine wrote without reading it. Only 45% of those developers think AI code is even functionally correct, and the share who say they always check it before committing still dropped from 48% to 39% in a year. 76% admit they generate AI code faster than they can verify it.

That's where the old-school programmer comes back in. By this summer, software job postings on Indeed were up almost 15% since Claude Code launched, while postings overall fell 7%. 71% of that rebound went to senior roles, mostly people who know the new tools too. Knowing what's actually happening underneath, the same skill the priesthood guarded, is what checking all that code takes.

Grace Hopper had the answer in the 1950s. She wanted people to write programs in plain English, and she was told computers didn't understand English. She died in 1992, about 30 years before they did.

full_text_zh:
约翰·冯·诺依曼帮助发明了现代计算机，当他的一名研究生让编程变得更容易时，他感到非常愤怒。

学生唐·吉利斯 (Don Gillies) 在普林斯顿大学的冯·诺依曼机器上手工将程序翻译成二进制。因此，他编写了一个程序来为他进行翻译，他后来说这是第一个汇编程序。冯·诺依曼告诉他，你不会使用有价值的科学计算仪器来进行文书工作。

老实说，在 20 世纪 50 年代初，他说得有道理。那时机器是很珍贵的东西，研究生的下午几乎是空闲的。

数学翻转得很快。 IBM FORTRAN 团队的领导者 John Backus 后来写道，到 1954 年，计算机中心的程序员的成本通常至少与计算机本身一样高，并且机器四分之一到一半的时间都花在了调试代码上。人类的时间已经成为值得拯救的东西。

因此，巴科斯的团队构建了一种语言，您可以在其中编写接近代数的内容，然后由机器编写代码。许多经验丰富的程序员讨厌它。巴克斯说，他们中的许多人将自己视为“神职人员”，守护技能对于普通人来说过于复杂。他还写道，他们正确地将自己的作品视为一种创造性艺术，他认真对待这一点。他的团队确信 FORTRAN 永远不会流行起来，除非它的程序几乎和手工编码的程序一样高效，所以这就是他们大部分努力的方向。一旦交付，人们就可以不再担心底层的机器代码。今天工作的大多数程序员从未阅读过他们的代码变成的程序集。

这就是这个视频要问的问题。每种编程语言的目标是什么？

现在在 Anthropic 工作的 Karpathy 一月份发帖称，他“现在主要用英语编程”，并承认这有点伤害自尊。在 Sonar 的新调查中，开发人员表示，他们提交的代码中约有 65% 由人工智能编写或大力协助，高于一年前的 42%。

所以我们回到了 1957 年，争论是否可以在不阅读机器所写内容的情况下相信它。只有 45% 的开发人员认为 AI 代码在功能上是正确的，而表示在提交之前总是进行检查的开发人员比例在一年内仍然从 48% 下降到 39%。 76% 的人承认他们生成人工智能代码的速度比验证代码的速度快。

这就是老派程序员回归的地方。到今年夏天，自 Claude Code 推出以来，Indeed 上的软件职位发布量增加了近 15%，而总体职位发布量下降了 7%。 71% 的反弹流向了高级职位，其中大多数人也了解新工具。知道底层实际发生了什么，这与祭司所守护的技能相同，也是检查所有代码所需要的。

格蕾丝·霍珀 (Grace Hopper) 在 20 世纪 50 年代找到了答案。她希望人们用简单的英语编写程序，但她被告知计算机听不懂英语。她于 1992 年去世，比他们早了大约 30 年。

title_en:
This Anthropic harness paper is f*cking gold

Anthropic's Labs team handed Claude one sentence and got a full app back 6 hours later. And the model wasn't the upgrade.

The upgrade: three agents, and none of them grades its own work.

prompt → spec → contract → build → QA → fix

The 6 parts of the harness:

Part 1 → planner

1-4 sentences in, a 16-feature spec out.
Product level only, no implementation details.

Part 2 → sprint contract

Before any code, the generator and the evaluator agree on "done".
In files, back and forth.

Part 3 → generator

One feature per sprint.
Self-check, then hand off to QA.

Part 4 → evaluator

Clicks through the running app with Playwright.
Sprint 3 alone had 27 criteria.

Part 5 → hard thresholds

Depth, functionality, design, code.
One score under the bar → the sprint fails.

Part 6 → cost

Solo: 20 min, $9, the game ignored input.
Harness: 6 hr, $200, the game was playable.

An agent that grades itself always passes. A stranger with Playwright doesn't.

I packed all 6 parts into one prompt. Drop it into Claude Code and it sets the harness up for you.

3 agents. 1 prompt. 0 self-grading.

title_en:
🚨 Your "deleted" photos might not be deleted.

Claude Code just found years of them hiding in a cache on my iPhone.

It started as a routine backup. I plugged my iPhone into my MacBook, and while it ran, I had Claude Code do a quick security check. It flagged something I wasn't even looking for: a directory called PhotoData/Thumbnails.

Inside were thousands of files. Photos, videos, screenshots. And a lot of them were things I had deleted.

Pictures from a couple of years ago. Screenshots I'd snapped and trashed seconds later. Even items I had cleared out of Recently Deleted. Some were still sitting right there.

Here's a sample of what I found:

→ Old screenshots of banking apps
→ Photos I deleted right after taking them
→ Random shots I never wanted on my phone
→ A few things I clearly remember deleting more than once

Here's what's going on. When you delete a photo, iOS removes it from your camera roll and from Recently Deleted. But it keeps a compressed copy in a Spotlight search cache, so your phone can still find things when you search. And that cache doesn't get fully cleared.

So I checked which apps had Files and Folders access. There were more than I expected, including apps I'd downloaded ages ago and completely forgotten about. Any of them could potentially read files from that cache.

I went through the list and revoked access for most of them.

The prompt I used is below. If you already have a backup, it takes just a few minutes.

Now I'm curious: how many apps on your phone have Files access right now?

title:

Actum's PoHA runs in production in two completely diffe
title_en:
One Ledger, Two Very Different Industries — How Does That Work?

Actum's PoHA runs in production in two completely different settings: a rail transit equipment manufacturer, with 5,000+ machines and operators doing hourly inspections; and a commercial hospitality setting, with guest data and service records flowing back and forth.

What the two settings need looks nothing alike — the factory needs every bolt's inspection tied to a person; the hotel needs every data access traceable. But underneath, the problem is the same: when an action happens, who was there, who authorized it, can you trace it afterward, can you hold someone accountable?

PoHA's answer is one shared ledger: Humans, Machines, and AI Agents, verified against the same standard, speaking through the same evidence. A pre-frozen codebook before the action, six-dimensional verification at the gate, signed attestation after — a factory inspection check-in and a hotel data access go through the same process.

The numbers: the ledger now produces ~5,800 verified events a day across 5,300+ endpoints, with 174,000+ on-chain attestations in the past 30 days, 0 failures, 99.986% coverage.

Different industries, same ledger. That's why PoHA can move from one setting to another: it doesn't solve one industry's business problem. It solves the problem every industry shares — who is accountable for what AI does.

title: Two days ago, we published our report on Anthropic’s IPO, drawing on research involving more than 80 enterprise customer
title_en:
Two days ago, we published our report on Anthropic’s IPO, drawing on research involving more than 80 enterprise customers. One interesting finding is that enterprise adoption may be slower than the market expects, particularly between now and the end of the first half of next year. Adoption could start to accelerate around the middle of next year.

The 58 traditional enterprises we track generally expect AI spending growth to slow in 2027. A closer look at their spending mix and project pipelines suggests that growth is shifting from paid seats to more complex applications, rather than demand reaching a ceiling.

On average, respondents expect AI spending to rise about 31% year over year in 2027. Roughly 60% expect slower growth next year than this year, and a small number expect spending to be flat or decline.

title_en:
Giving an AI agent access to capital is one thing. Giving it a defined budget, a limited session and a clear strategy to follow is another.

I was looking into @termix_ai’s BNB Chain Quant Agent, and the structure stood out. Users choose a trading strategy, set a capital limit and a time period, then let the agent operate through a wallet created specifically for that job. The session can be revoked at any time.

What I find interesting is how the roles are separated: one side provides the capital, another provides the strategy, and the agent handles execution within the assigned limits.

That lets strategy providers and capital owners work together without handing an agent unlimited access to funds.

I think that’s a more practical direction for agent-based DeFi than fully open-ended autonomy.

But limits protect against runaway access, not against a bad strategy. The real question is how these strategies perform over time, not just how easily an agent can execute trades.

Would you let an agent trade with your capital under a strict limit, and what would you want to see first?

我发现有趣的是角色是如何分离的：一侧提供资本，另一侧提供策略，代理在指定的限制内处理执行。

我认为对于基于代理的 DeFi 来说，这是比完全开放式自治更实用的方向。

title:
Same agent ID. Different model. Same reputation?

Here's an interesting problem I've been thinking about while exploring
title_en:
Same agent ID. Different model. Same reputation?

Here's an interesting problem I've been thinking about while exploring @termix_ai and ERC-8004.

Imagine an AI agent that has completed 500 jobs with a 98% success rate.

Pretty solid track record, right?

Now imagine its developer replaces the underlying model, changes its tools and completely rewrites how it executes tasks.

The agent still has the same onchain identity.

But is it really the same agent you trusted yesterday?

This is where AI agent versioning gets interesting.

ERC-8004 provides a framework for persistent agent identities and reputation signals, but an identity alone doesn't tell you whether the software behind it has changed.

And that's a pretty important distinction.

I think future agent marketplaces should make it easier to track:

❯ Model versions and major updates
❯ Changes to tools and execution environments
❯ Performance before and after upgrades
❯ Which version actually completed each job

This matters for something like TermiX's AACP, where agents can provide services, build reputation and participate in onchain transactions.

A reputation score earned by version 1.0 shouldn't automatically guarantee that version 2.0 performs just as well.

Of course, updates can make agents significantly better.

The point isn't to discourage upgrades.

It's to make sure reputation reflects what an agent can actually deliver today, not just what an older version achieved months ago.

Because a persistent identity is valuable.

But a verifiable history of what changed behind that identity could be even more useful.

title_en:
There are 3 ways to use AI effectively.

1. Automation

You know exactly what you want to achieve. You give AI clear instructions, and it handles the task for you.

2. Augmentation

You’re still figuring things out. You use AI to brainstorm, explore ideas, solve problems and think through possibilities. You and AI work together.

3. Agency

You give AI a goal, the necessary knowledge and responsibilities, and it works independently on your behalf.

For example, an AI agent that handles customer enquiries 24/7 without you having to respond to every message manually.

Automation gets things done. Augmentation helps you think better. Agency gives AI the ability to act independently.

Learning when and how to use all three is where the real advantage lies.

title:

The growing number of vulnerabilities discovered in open s
title_en:
I think there’s a major misunderstanding in this discussion.

The growing number of vulnerabilities discovered in open source software doesn’t necessarily mean that open source code is worse than proprietary software.

What we’re seeing is a massive increase in scrutiny.

For years, many open source projects simply didn’t receive thorough security reviews. Nobody had the time, resources or financial incentive to look that closely.

Now anyone with access to a capable LLM can point it at a public repository and start looking for vulnerabilities. And newer models are getting remarkably good at finding issues that previous tools and human reviewers missed.

But something very similar is happening behind closed doors.

I can tell you from our own experience, and from discussions with people at other software companies, that internal development teams are also struggling with a flood of findings from AI-assisted code reviews.

Many of these findings concern code that has been running in production for years. In proprietary software development, they rarely become public CVEs or security advisories. They end up as Jira tickets, creating backlogs that take weeks or months to process.

Ironically, while AI accelerates software development, it’s also slowing teams down by exposing years of accumulated technical debt and security issues that nobody had identified before.

So I’d be careful about interpreting the current wave of open source vulnerabilities as evidence of lower code quality.

full_text_zh:
我认为这次讨论存在重大误解。

开源软件中发现的漏洞数量不断增加并不一定意味着开源代码比专有软件更糟糕。

我们看到的是审查的大幅增加。

多年来，许多开源项目根本没有接受彻底的安全审查。没有人有时间、资源或经济动力来仔细观察。

现在，任何有权访问有能力的法学硕士的人都可以将其指向公共存储库并开始寻找漏洞。较新的模型非常擅长发现以前的工具和人工审核人员遗漏的问题。

但非常相似的事情正在幕后发生。

我可以根据我们自己的经验以及与其他软件公司人员的讨论告诉您，内部开发团队也在努力应对人工智能辅助代码审查的大量发现。

其中许多发现涉及已在生产环境中运行多年的代码。在专有软件开发中，它们很少成为公共 CVE 或安全公告。它们最终会成为 Jira 票证，造成积压，需要数周或数月的时间才能处理。

具有讽刺意味的是，虽然人工智能加速了软件开发，但它也暴露了多年来积累的技术债务和以前没有人发现的安全问题，从而减慢了团队的速度。

因此，我会谨慎地将当前的开源漏洞浪潮解释为代码质量较低的证据。

title_en:
Opening A Position Is Easy, Managing It Is Where Things Get Complicated.

Anyone who has used lending protocols knows the position doesn't manage itself.

You have to keep track of collateral, monitor your Health Factor, understand how much borrowing room remains and react when market conditions change.

That ongoing responsibility is one of the more interesting problems AI agents could help address.

@meetmotes has now integrated with @aave, extending its agents into decentralised lending and borrowing.

The integration introduces capabilities around:

➠ Collateral management: Helping manage collateral as lending positions evolve.

➠ Borrowing and repayment: Automating parts of the borrowing process and repayment.

➠ Health Factor monitoring: Tracking position health and applying automated risk controls.

What makes this particularly relevant to Motes is the connection to Genesis NFTs. 

Each Genesis NFT is designed to link its owner to a dedicated AI Agent, with personalised DeFi strategies operating within permissions defined by the owner.

title_en:
I came across an interesting finding in yesterday’s @databricks announcement.

After studying more than 80,000 customer pipeline issues, the company found that over half required knowledge specific to the organization to resolve.

And I think there’s a much bigger business lesson hiding in that number.

When we talk about AI agents, we often focus on what they can do.

Can they write content?

Can they analyze data?

Can they manage workflows?

Can they complete tasks without constant human involvement?

Those are useful questions.

But there’s another one I find increasingly important as we build CAIS.

Does the agent actually understand the business it’s working for?

Imagine two companies using exactly the same AI tools.

One wants to increase sales as quickly as possible.

The other is prioritizing profitability, customer retention and protecting its brand positioning.

An agent might recommend the same aggressive discount campaign to both.

The recommendation could be technically sound.

But it wouldn’t necessarily be right for both businesses.

That’s the difference between having access to information and understanding business context.

It’s also why we’re building CAIS around the idea of One Brand Brain.

The goal is to bring business strategy, knowledge, people and AI workflows into a more coherent operating environment.

Not because every decision should be automated.

Quite the opposite.

Because businesses need to know which decisions can be delegated, which require additional context and which should remain firmly in human hands.

I think we’ll see increasingly capable agents over the coming months.

But capability alone won’t determine which businesses benefit most.

The companies that understand their own processes, priorities and decision-making responsibilities will be in a much stronger position to use that capability effectively.

Sometimes the most valuable thing you can give an AI agent isn’t another tool.

It’s a better understanding of the business.

当我们谈论人工智能代理时，我们经常关注它们能做什么。

他们可以写内容吗？

他们可以分析数据吗？

他们可以管理工作流程吗？

它们能否在没有人类持续参与的情况下完成任务？

这些都是有用的问题。

但我发现，随着我们建立 CAIS，还有一个问题变得越来越重要。

代理人是否真正了解其所从事的业务？

想象一下两家公司使用完全相同的人工智能工具。

人们希望尽快增加销售额。

另一个是优先考虑盈利能力、客户保留和保护其品牌定位。

代理商可能会向两者推荐相同的激进折扣活动。

该建议在技术上可能是合理的。

但这不一定适合两家企业。

这就是获取信息和了解业务环境之间的区别。

这也是我们围绕同一个品牌大脑的理念构建 CAIS 的原因。

目标是将业务战略、知识、人员和人工智能工作流程带入一个更加一致的操作环境中。

并不是因为每个决定都应该自动化。

恰恰相反。

因为企业需要知道哪些决策可以委托，哪些需要额外的背景信息，哪些应该牢牢掌握在人手中。

我认为在接下来的几个月里我们会看到能力越来越强的特工。

但仅凭能力并不能决定哪些企业受益最多。

了解自己的流程、优先事项和决策责任的公司将能够更有效地利用这种能力。

有时，你能为人工智能代理提供的最有价值的东西并不是其他工具。

这是对业务的更好理解。

但仅凭能力并不能决定哪些企业受益最多。

了解自己的流程、优先事项和决策责任的公司将能够更有效地利用这种能力。

有时，你能为人工智能代理提供的最有价值的东西并不是其他工具。

这是对业务的更好理解。
